opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd describe it is that my numbers have drifted somewhat earlier over time, but not in a dramatic way. A lot of it is just more evidence about how far you get by scaling things up.

If you go back maybe ten years, I'd have said something like: there's a reasonable chance this deep learning stuff goes all the way, but it's pretty uncertain, and it might be one more paradigm among many that hits a wall. Since then we've watched a few orders of magnitude of scale-up, and the systems have just kept getting better in a fairly predictable way. That's pushed up the probability that you don't need many new ideas, that it's mostly a question of compute, data, and some engineering.

So in terms of concrete numbers: when I think about AI that's capable enough to, roughly, be building a Dyson sphere, systems that could do essentially everything humans do and are driving the trajectory of civilization, I'd put something like 15% on that by 2030 and maybe 40% by 2040. Those aren't super precise. If you'd asked me a few years ago, the 2030 number would have been lower, maybe high single digits, and the 2040 number somewhat lower too.

The other thing that's changed is less about the headline numbers and more about the shape of the distribution. I now put more weight on a world where things are fairly continuous. You see increasingly impressive systems, they get deployed, they have a big economic impact, and then you get to the point where AI is accelerating AI research and things speed up a lot. I put less weight on worlds where nothing happens and then suddenly something happens.

And I'd say there's a lot of uncertainty in both directions. Scaling could slow down: we could run into limits on how much money people are willing to spend, or on data, or the remaining gaps like long-horizon agency and reliability could turn out harder than they look. Or it could go faster than I'm expecting. I try not to update too hard on any single impressive demo, because people, including me, have a tendency to overreact to them. But the cumulative evidence has moved me toward shorter timelines, and I think that's the right direction to have moved.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that my timelines have gotten shorter, but maybe less dramatically than people would guess from the outside. If you'd asked me around 2016 or 2017, I would have put something like a 15 or 20 percent chance on transformative AI by 2030, and maybe 40 or 50 percent by 2040. And by transformative I mean something that actually changes the growth rate of the world, not just a cool chatbot. Right now I'd say those numbers have moved up. I'd put maybe 30 percent on 2030 and something like 60 percent on 2040. Those aren't precise, but that's roughly the shape of the update.

The thing I find more interesting than the numbers is what drove the change. It wasn't really that I was surprised by scaling as such. I had already thought that if you just made models much bigger and trained them on much more data, they would get a lot better, and that the compute to do that was going to become available. What surprised me was how far you could get before you had to do anything clever. I expected more of the progress to come from algorithmic insight and more of it to look like fragile, domain-specific systems. Instead you've got these very general models where a huge fraction of the capability comes from a pretty simple recipe. That pushes me toward thinking the remaining gap is smaller than I'd assumed, because it means fewer independent breakthroughs are needed.

The other thing that happened is just that the economic side became real. In 2017 you had to argue that someone would eventually spend tens of billions of dollars on a training run. Now that's not a hypothetical, it's a line item. So a lot of the uncertainty I had about whether the world would actually bother to scale has collapsed. That matters a lot for timelines, because a big chunk of my earlier probability mass was on "the technology works but nobody invests fast enough."

Where I haven't updated as much is on the hard tail. There's still a real chance that the current paradigm plateaus, or that the things that are hard for these systems, like long-horizon agency and reliability, turn out to be genuinely difficult rather than just the next thing scale solves. I don't think I know how to put a tight bound on that. So my distribution has shifted earlier and gotten a bit tighter, but I still have real probability on 2050 and beyond. I try to be careful about not just extrapolating the vibe of the last three years, because the last three years were partly a catch-up on compute that had been sitting unused.

I'd also say I'm a little wary of how I frame these updates. It's easy to tell a story afterward that makes it sound like you saw it coming. I didn't see the specifics coming. What I think I got roughly right was the general shape, that progress would be driven by compute and would look continuous rather than a sudden jump. What I got wrong was the pace and how little architectural novelty it would take.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between my overall timelines and my probability of very short timelines. You can become substantially more worried about AI by 2030 without moving your median forecast by that much. You’re moving probability from later dates into the next few years, but there’s still a lot of uncertainty about what happens if the current approach runs into difficulties.

The main question is how much work remains between systems that look impressive and systems that can actually automate a large fraction of research. If that gap is small, progress could be very fast, especially once AI starts accelerating AI development. If it requires important additional ideas, then you have a much wider distribution over when those ideas arrive.

So I wouldn’t interpret changes in my forecasts as just, ‘Models got better, therefore subtract five years.’ It’s more about updating on which world we’re in: how far the existing methods can take us, how much additional work is needed, and how quickly that work can be done. The 2030 forecast is particularly sensitive to those questions. By 2040, you’ve allowed more time for several different paths to work.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish two things: how my timelines have changed, and how much confidence I put in those timelines. I don’t have a precise record in front of me of what probability I assigned to each date, so I don’t want to invent a history where I was consistently updating in some particular direction.

But the basic tension is that you see progress, which makes the whole project look more plausible, and at the same time you learn more about what’s hard. You can think, “These systems are much more capable than I expected,” while also thinking, “Getting from here to a system that can reliably do a long, complicated research project may require more work than I appreciated.” Those updates can partly cancel.

For 2030, the details of that transition matter a lot. Do current approaches extend far enough? How quickly can you turn impressive capabilities into useful work? By 2040, there’s more room for approaches to change and for people to solve problems that would delay things beyond 2030. So I’d generally expect my probability for 2030 to be more sensitive to the particular picture I have of how development proceeds.

And I’d be cautious about treating a forecast as a very crisp belief. There’s a big difference between having a model that puts substantial probability on advanced AI by some date and feeling like you understand the path that gets you there.
